# AI Coding Research Brief - November 27, 2026

**Coverage window:** November 20-27, 2026. Five new papers were selected after checking the prior Quadratus digests through November 20. All five are newly posted arXiv preprints; treat the reported results as author-reported, not independent replications. The proposed experiments are research suggestions only and do not authorize implementation.

## 1. Improving Repair Agents with Cause-Chain Diagnoses (FORECAST)
**November 23, 2026 - [arXiv:2611.30574](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30574)**

FORECAST compares executions of passing and failing tests and extracts a short cause chain: conditions, state changes, or data-flow features that explain where the failing execution diverges. It appends that diagnosis to the issue prompt, so an existing repair agent can use it without changing its own harness.

On all 300 SWE-bench Lite issues, the authors evaluated five repair-agent configurations with Claude Haiku 4.5 and Qwen3.5. Across agents, the resolved-issue share rose from 48.5% to 70.9% for Haiku and from 31.2% to 56.1% for Qwen. The reported gains persisted across repeated runs and also helped agents that already executed the tests used to derive the diagnosis.

**Why it matters:** It gives a repair worker evidence about the causal failure path instead of asking it to reconstruct that path from a symptom and a large repository. It is a potentially model-agnostic way to improve handoffs between a diagnostic specialist and an implementer.

**Limitations:** The evidence is from one benchmark of 300 issues and two model families. The benefit depends on having useful passing and failing executions; transfer to Quadratus tasks, other languages, and more complex test environments remains unmeasured.

**Quadratus experiment:** Add a read-only diagnostic stage that runs the baseline and relevant passing/failing tests, then returns a compact cause chain with implicated files, predicates, state/data-flow evidence, and the reproducing test. Give that packet to the repair worker. Compare it with an ordinary issue-only handoff under the same total budget. Measure verified fixes, localization accuracy, repair iterations, and cost.

## 2. SpecEngineeringBench: Evaluating Coding Agents as Autonomous Specification Engineers
**November 24, 2026 - [arXiv:2611.32973](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32973)**

SpecEngineeringBench tests whether agents can decide what to test and where to investigate from functional requirements, rather than being handed an issue description, test entry point, or files to inspect. It contains 100 multi-defect instances from 78 open-source Python repositories across 16 application categories. Separate tasks assess autonomous test-suite generation and defect discovery through execution analysis.

Across seven coding agents, the authors report a 91.47% Head Pass Rate and 80.48% change-focused coverage, but only a 26.36% Fail-to-Pass Rate. Localization recall falls from 78.11% at file level to 51.29% at function level. Agent-generated tests improve file, function, and hunk localization recall by 4.99, 2.77, and 2.69 percentage points over using the repository's existing tests alone.

**Why it matters:** Passing tests and high coverage do not prove that a test suite exposes the defects that matter. A dedicated specification-engineering role could produce stronger acceptance evidence before implementation begins.

**Limitations:** This is a new benchmark with 100 instances, limited to Python repositories. Its results may not transfer to other languages, proprietary codebases, or tasks whose requirements are less explicit.

**Quadratus experiment:** Give a read-only specification engineer the request and repository, but no implementation diff or suggested test location. Require it to produce requirement-linked tests and a defect-exposure report. Evaluate test validity, known-defect detection, mutation score, and localization separately; do not use line coverage as a proxy for defect exposure.

## 3. MeterRouter: Budget-Aware Dynamic Routing for Multi-Agent Systems
**November 25, 2026 - [arXiv:2611.34327](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34327)**

MeterRouter constructs a collaboration graph incrementally for each query. It jointly chooses each agent's role, model, incoming communication links, and when to stop, using a live per-query monetary budget. The router is trained from successful workflow examples and refined with reinforcement learning that rewards correct answers while penalizing cost and budget overruns.

Across five benchmarks (MMLU-Pro, MuSR, BBEH, Omni-MATH-2, and MBPP+), it reports 66.72% average accuracy at about $0.00256 per query, compared with 66.80% at about $0.01415 for MasRouter. That is approximately 82% lower average cost at nearly equal aggregate accuracy. At the tested budgets, at least 99.98% of queries stayed within budget.

**Why it matters:** Quadratus should not assume that every task needs the same number of agents, model strength, or communication pattern. The useful principle is to allocate remaining budget after observing actual prior-call costs and outputs, rather than choosing a fixed team up front.

**Limitations:** Only 138 test queries were used for the code-generation benchmark MBPP+; most evaluation is general or mathematical reasoning. The three model backbones were gpt-oss-20b, gpt-oss-120b, and MiniMax-M3, not subscription coding CLIs. The reported 82% saving is not a forecast for Quadratus.

**Quadratus experiment:** Compare the current fixed four-phase workflow with a simple budget-aware policy: one lead by default, cheaper read-only scouts for separable work, stronger specialists only when evidence warrants them, and an explicit reserve for integration and verification. Record per-agent cost, communication tokens, verified success, and budget compliance. Start with rules before attempting to train a router.

## 4. Spec-Test Coverage Gap: Detecting Overspecified Tests in SWE-Bench-Style Benchmarks
**November 24, 2026 - [arXiv:2611.31839](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31839)**

This paper studies tests that enforce implementation details not required by the task specification, causing valid alternative patches to fail. It introduces a Spec-Test Coverage Gap score and flags a task when two LLM judges both rate the test as overspecified.

On 206 validation tasks with prior human-audit labels, the judges identified 89% of tasks known to be overspecified and incorrectly flagged 4% of tasks known to be fine. Applied to SWE-bench Verified and public SWE-bench Pro, the method flagged 23% and 35% of tasks, respectively. In a follow-up involving 2,186 failed patches, relaxing the flagged tests allowed 61% of those patches to pass; the authors estimate that benchmark resolve rates could rise by up to 12 percentage points.

**Why it matters:** A verifier can reject a correct implementation because it tests the reference patch rather than the stated requirement. Quadratus needs to distinguish genuine regressions from tests that encode undocumented choices.

**Limitations:** The judge is an LLM-based audit, not a formal proof of specification equivalence. The validation set is 206 tasks, the benchmark analysis focuses on SWE-bench, and the follow-up relaxation is itself model-mediated. A relaxed test passing does not independently prove that the alternative is correct.

**Quadratus experiment:** Add an independent requirement-to-test audit to acceptance review. For each assertion, identify the explicit requirement it protects and whether a materially different valid implementation should pass. Classify tests as under-specified, aligned, or over-specified. Never relax an acceptance test automatically; require independent review and a valid alternative implementation.

## 5. HoMe: Toward Practical Harness Optimization of Memory Systems for AI Assistants
**November 25, 2026 - [arXiv:2611.34624](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34624)**

HoMe treats memory as a versioned system whose construction, maintenance, retrieval, prompts, and configuration can be optimized through evidence. It commits memory state after each session, traces failures to determine whether information was never written, later overwritten, not retrieved, or misused, and separates detailed case diagnosis from mechanism-level optimization. It reduces evaluation cost with smoke tests, structural candidate gates, adaptive sampling, and reuse of unchanged memory construction.

On the ReMe memory system, six formal candidate evaluations per benchmark improved LongMemEval-S from 0.888 to 0.916 while reducing query-time tokens from 43.9K to 17.9K (59% fewer). On BEAM-1M, the score rose from 0.650 to 0.704 while tokens fell from 101.8K to 60.4K (41% fewer), despite test histories averaging about eight times the length of the BEAM-100K training histories.

**Why it matters:** It offers a practical method for diagnosing persistent-context failures without loading every prior session into one agent's context. The separation between per-case diagnosticians and a mechanism-level optimizer is also relevant to Quadratus's shared memory and run-ledger design.

**Limitations:** The experiments use one memory framework and two memory benchmarks, with a fixed model setup and an LLM judge. BEAM-1M contains only 35 cases, and some question categories declined even as aggregate scores improved. This is not a direct evaluation of repository/code memory.

**Quadratus experiment:** Version task memory and key run artifacts per session. When a later worker fails, trace whether the necessary fact was absent, overwritten, not retrieved, or misapplied. Have independent case diagnosticians return compact evidence packets; let a separate optimizer propose one mechanism-level change. Evaluate on held-out tasks and track both answer quality and context tokens.

## The single most promising idea to try

**Add an evidence-backed cause-chain diagnostic handoff before repair.** Use passing and failing executions to identify where behavior diverges, then give the repair worker a compact causal packet rather than only the issue text. This is bounded, can be tested without changing the coding agents, and has the strongest direct coding-agent result in this week's set. Compare it against the current handoff on a fixed task set and equal total budgets, using independent tests to measure verified fixes rather than accepted-looking patches.
